newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian royalists formally launch alliance.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian royalists formally launch alliance.

text.p: Cambodia's ruling FUNCINPEC party on Thursday formally launched a political alliance with three other parties in a move that was likely to further strain ties with its coalition government partner.
Cambodian co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh, leader of the royalist FUNCINPEC, was appointed president of the National United Front (NUF) at a meeting in Phnom Penh.
Hundreds of supporters, several diplomats and Khmer Rouge defectors who have voiced support for the alliance attended the ceremony.
The NUF brings together FUNCINPEC, the officially unrecognised opposition Khmer Nation Party (KNP), a wing of the divided Buddhist Liberal Democratic Party (BLDP) and the small Khmer Neutral Party.
"The front is becoming one of the major political forces in the country...the strongest political force," Ranariddh said after leaders of the four groups signed a 14-point platform.

The NUF faces a burgeoning alliance among co-Premier Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) -- FUNCINPEC's partner in the government but also its main political rival -- and the Liberal Democratic Party and another wing of the BLDP.

Some analysts believed the alliances would worsen relations between the CPP and FUNCINPEC, who formed their uneasy coalition following U.N.-run elections in 1993, ahead of local and general elections due in 1998.

Ties worsened over Ranariddh's demand last year for a greater share of power to reflect his party's narrow election win, and have been further strained by their efforts to win the allegiance of thousands of Khmer Rouge defectors.

Sok Pheap, a former Khmer Rouge commander who split with hardliners and has since been appointed a general in the royal armed forces, told the meeting the NUF had the support of a group set up by defectors in the northwest called the Democratic National Union Movement.
But the Khmer Rouge movement did not formally join the front and has said it would not take sides.
The Khmer Rouge, held responsible for the deaths of more than one million people during its brutal 1975-79 rule, reneged on a U.N.-brokered 1991 peace pact and had been fighting the ruling coalition.
But the Maoist group has lost power as a fighting force following mass defections last August.
The NUF manifesto, among other things, pledged to support the country's constitutional monarchy and work for free and fair general polls in 1998 that would elect only one prime minister.
